Let \(V=\mathbb F_2^6\). The exact number is

\[
\boxed{2}.
\]

A concise classification is as follows.

Fix a common Lagrangian \(U\), choose a complement \(X\), and write matrices in blocks \(V=U\oplus X\). Since every form in \(W\) vanishes on \(U\times U\), each matrix has form

\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}
0&M\\
M^T&C
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad C\in \operatorname{Alt}_3(2).
\]

Such a matrix is invertible iff \(M\) is invertible. Hence the projection \(A\mapsto M\) identifies \(W\) with a \(3\)-dimensional subspace \(S\le M_3(\mathbb F_2)\) whose nonzero elements are all invertible.

Up to left-right equivalence, there is only one such \(S\): it is the regular representation of \(\mathbb F_8\). Indeed, after multiplying on the left we may assume \(I\in S\). Then every nonzero \(T\in S\setminus\{I\}\) has neither \(0\) nor \(1\) as an eigenvalue, so its minimal polynomial is irreducible cubic and \(T\) has order \(7\). The resulting \(8\)-element linear spread set is therefore the field spread, i.e.

\[
S=\{L_a:a\in\mathbb F_8\},
\]

where \(L_a(x)=ax\).

Using the trace pairing on \(\mathbb F_8\), every such \(W\) can then be written as

\[
\omega_a((u,x),(v,y))
=
\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb F_8/\mathbb F_2}\bigl(a(uy+vx)\bigr)
+
\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb F_8/\mathbb F_2}
\bigl(\lambda(a)(xy^2+x^2y)\bigr),
\]

for an \(\mathbb F_2\)-linear map \(\lambda:\mathbb F_8\to \mathbb F_8\).

Changing the complement \(X\) by a shear replaces \(\lambda\) by

\[
\lambda(a)+qa+sa^2.
\]

Since every \(\mathbb F_2\)-linear map \(\mathbb F_8\to\mathbb F_8\) has the form

\[
\lambda(a)=\alpha a+\beta a^2+\gamma a^4,
\]

only the coefficient of \(a^4\) remains as an invariant. Thus every \(W\) is equivalent to exactly one of the forms

\[
\lambda(a)=0
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\lambda(a)=a^4,
\]

because the nonzero coefficient can be scaled to \(1\).

These two cases are not equivalent. If \(\lambda=0\), then \(W\) has many common Lagrangians: every \(\mathbb F_8\)-line in \(\mathbb F_8^2\) is common Lagrangian, giving \(9\) of them.

If \(\lambda(a)=a^4\), then the original \(U\) is the unique common Lagrangian. Indeed, any other common Lagrangian must be the graph of an \(\mathbb F_2\)-linear map \(h:\mathbb F_8\to\mathbb F_8\). The isotropy condition gives, for all \(x,y\),

\[
h(x)y+h(y)x=x^2y^4+x^4y^2.
\]

Putting \(y=1\) forces

\[
h(x)=x^4+x^2+cx.
\]

Substituting this back gives

\[
x^4y+xy^4+x^2y+xy^2=x^2y^4+x^4y^2,
\]

which is false for all \(x,y\in\mathbb F_8\). Hence no such second Lagrangian exists.

Therefore the two normal forms lie in distinct \(GL_6(2)\)-orbits, and they exhaust all possibilities.

\[
\boxed{2}
\]
